lessons.title: China's Yuan and the Push for De-dollarization

body.text: China is the world's second-largest economy and its largest trading nation, and its currency still holds barely 2 to 3% of global reserves. That gap is not an accident, it is a direct choice, and understanding why reveals exactly what Chapter 1's four requirements actually demand.

children.text: Lesson 1 showed the euro coming closest to matching the dollar's institutional depth, yet still falling short structurally. China's yuan, also called the renminbi, tells a different story: an economy easily large enough to support a major reserve currency, held back not by fragmentation but by deliberate policy choices Beijing itself has made, and has only partially started to unwind.
From Managed Currency to Aspiring Global Player

markDefs.definition: Government-imposed restrictions on how freely money can move into and out of a country, limiting foreigners' ability to freely buy, sell, or move a currency and its domestic assets.

children.text: For decades, China kept the yuan tightly managed: its exchange rate set daily by the People's Bank of China within a narrow trading band, and strict

limiting how freely money could move in and out of the country. This directly violates Chapter 1's first requirement for reserve currency status, full convertibility, and it was a deliberate choice, not an oversight; Beijing prioritised control over its exchange rate and financial system above the benefits of full convertibility. That began shifting, cautiously, after the 2008 global financial crisis, which China watched originate inside the dollar-centred financial system it depended on, and decided it needed options beyond near-total dollar reliance.

events.title: First Cross-Border Trade Settlement
events.description: China began allowing select trade with Hong Kong and ASEAN partners to be settled directly in yuan rather than routed through dollars.

events.title: CIPS Launched
events.description: China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System went live, a domestic alternative to SWIFT for yuan-denominated transactions, covered in Chapter 3.

events.title: Yuan Joins the IMF's SDR Basket
events.description: The yuan was formally added to the IMF's Special Drawing Rights basket with roughly an 11% weighting, the third-largest at inclusion behind the dollar and euro, a major symbolic milestone.

events.title: Yuan-Denominated Oil Futures Launch
events.description: The Shanghai International Energy Exchange began trading crude oil futures priced in yuan, quickly nicknamed the petroyuan, a direct attempt to chip at the petrodollar system from Chapter 3, Lesson 2.

events.title: Russia Trade Shifts to Yuan
events.description: Cut off from large parts of the dollar system by sanctions, Russia shifted a large share of its trade with China into yuan and rubles rather than dollars.

children.text: Why the Yuan Hasn't Taken Off Despite China's Size

Chapter 1's four requirements, convertibility, deep capital markets, trust and rule of law, and network effects, map directly onto the yuan's specific limitations. Full convertibility remains restricted; foreign investors can access more of China's onshore bond and equity markets than a decade ago, through schemes like Bond Connect, but capital controls still limit how freely money moves in bulk. Trust in rule of law is a genuine concern for large foreign holders, given China's more opaque legal system and the state's ability to intervene directly in markets and companies. Network effects are the one area China has actively built, through CIPS, bilateral currency swap lines with dozens of central banks, and the petroyuan contracts, but starting decades behind an entrenched incumbent is a slow climb.

body.caption: The yuan against Chapter 1's four requirements

cells: Restricted; capital controls limit free movement despite gradual liberalisation like Bond Connect
Large and growing onshore markets, but foreign access remains partial and state-influenced
Trust in institutions and rule of law
A genuine concern for large foreign holders given state intervention risk and legal opacity
Actively being built through CIPS, swap lines, and petroyuan contracts, but starting from a small base

body.text: This is the clearest illustration this course offers of Chapter 1's central claim: economic size alone does not confer reserve currency status. China chose control over its exchange rate and capital account over the network effects and trust that full convertibility would bring. That is a rational choice given Beijing's domestic priorities, but it is also a direct, self-imposed ceiling on how far the yuan can realistically go as a reserve currency without a fundamental policy shift.

children.text: China's push has fed into a broader conversation among BRICS members, Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and newer members, about reducing collective dependence on the dollar. Proposals for a shared BRICS currency have been discussed publicly, including at the 2023 BRICS summit, but no such currency actually exists or has launched. What has grown, more modestly, is bilateral local-currency trade settlement between individual BRICS members, exactly the kind of arrangement covered for China-Russia trade above and for India's own rupee mechanism in Chapter 3. It is worth being precise about this distinction: a shared BRICS currency remains a discussion point, not a functioning reality, while local-currency trade settlement between pairs of countries is already happening on a real, if still modest, scale.

India, despite sharing the BRICS table with China, has stayed notably cautious about yuan-led de-dollarization initiatives. Two practical reasons stand out. First, India runs one of its largest bilateral trade deficits with China, tens of billions of dollars a year, which makes India wary of any arrangement that could deepen its economic dependence on a strategic rival. Second, India and China have an active, unresolved border dispute and a broadly adversarial strategic relationship, which makes New Delhi reluctant to build financial infrastructure that China could influence or control. India's own approach, covered fully in Lesson 3, has instead focused on pursuing rupee internationalisation independently, through its own bilateral arrangements, rather than joining a yuan-centred bloc.

body.title: Would Full Convertibility Actually Help China?
body.scenario: A policy advisor in Beijing proposes fully liberalising the yuan, removing capital controls entirely and letting the exchange rate float freely, arguing this is the fastest way to boost the yuan's reserve currency status and catch up to the dollar and euro.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what would China gain from this move toward Chapter 1's convertibility requirement, and what genuine risks might make Beijing hesitant to adopt it despite the potential reserve currency benefits?
body.modelAnswer: Full convertibility would directly address the yuan's biggest gap against Chapter 1's four requirements, likely accelerating foreign central banks' willingness to hold yuan reserves and use it more widely in trade and lending, the same way it helped the dollar and euro. The risk Beijing weighs against this is real: removing capital controls would mean losing the tight grip the government currently holds over the exchange rate and domestic financial conditions, potentially exposing China to the kind of rapid capital flight and currency volatility that other emerging markets, including India during the 2013 taper tantrum from Chapter 1, have experienced. For a government that has consistently prioritised financial stability and control over global currency ambitions, that trade-off has so far tilted toward keeping the controls in place, even at the direct cost of the yuan's international standing.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What best explains why the yuan holds only about 2 to 3% of global reserves despite China being the world's second-largest economy?
options: China's economy is too small to support a major reserve currency
The IMF has refused to recognise the yuan as an official reserve asset
China has deliberately maintained capital controls and a managed exchange rate, prioritising financial control over full convertibility
The yuan has never been used in any cross-border trade settlement
body.explanation: China has deliberately kept capital controls and a managed exchange rate in place, prioritising control over its financial system over the full convertibility Chapter 1 identifies as essential for reserve currency status. This is a policy choice, not an economic constraint, which is exactly why it is unlikely to change without a fundamental shift in Beijing's priorities.

body.text: Reserve share figures, SDR basket weightings, and trade statistics in this lesson are presented as widely cited, rounded approximations for teaching purposes, drawn from IMF and other publicly reported data that is updated periodically. Discussion of a potential BRICS currency reflects publicly reported proposals as of this course's writing and should not be read as describing an existing currency. This lesson is educational content, not investment or policy advice.

points: China's yuan holds only about 2 to 3% of global reserves despite China's economic size, largely because Beijing has deliberately maintained capital controls and a managed exchange rate rather than full convertibility
China has actively built network effects since 2009 through cross-border trade settlement, CIPS, SDR basket inclusion in 2016, and yuan-denominated petroyuan oil futures from 2018
Mapped against Chapter 1's four requirements, the yuan is strongest on network effects and weakest on convertibility and trust in rule of law for large foreign holders
A shared BRICS currency remains a discussed proposal, not a functioning reality; bilateral local-currency trade settlement between individual BRICS members is the real, if still modest, trend

India has stayed deliberately cautious about yuan-led de-dollarization, given its large trade deficit with China and unresolved strategic tensions, choosing instead to pursue rupee internationalisation independently, the subject of this course's final lesson
